routes.description: Show that belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God does not accord with the available evidence because apparently gratuitous suffering and salvation-related confusion conflict with the expected conduct of such a deity, while the offered arguments from reason, design, morality, and purpose do not overcome those conflicts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence expected under an all-powerful, all-loving God is materially inconsistent with suffering or religious confusion and the affirmative grounds for theism remain insufficient to restore rational warrant.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the total available evidence makes belief in the specified all-powerful, all-loving God irrational.

centralBridges.description: Establish that apparently purposeless suffering is unexpected if an all-powerful and all-loving God exists.
Establish that serious consequences attached to disputed religious claims conflict with divine love and adequate revelation.
Show that arguments from reason, fine-tuning, morality, or purpose do not supply enough specific support for the specified God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Define rational belief as belief proportioned to the reason and evidence available to the believer.
Supply natural explanations for cognition, moral intuitions, or biological complexity where these are offered as evidence for God.

routes.description: Show that belief in God remains rational through a cumulative explanatory case from reliable reason, life-permitting order, objective morality, and human purpose, while accounting for suffering and other contrary evidence without requiring that every difficulty be conclusively resolved.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism provides material explanatory support across the principal affirmative issues and the alleged conflicts from evil or religious confusion do not defeat the resulting cumulative warrant.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the cumulative evidence and available answers to defeaters make belief in God rational.

centralBridges.description: Establish that reason, cosmic order, morality, and purpose jointly provide positive explanatory support for theism.
Show that suffering can count as counterevidence without rendering belief in an all-loving God irrational.
Show that objective goodness and obligation are more adequately grounded in God than in purposeless physical reality.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why designed intelligence supplies a basis for trusting human capacities to understand truth.
Relate divine intention, religious claims, and human significance to the broader rational case for theism.

sections.title: Rational warrant and trust in reason
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the evidential standard governing the motion and tests whether evolved cognition or divinely intended intelligence provides an adequate basis for trusting human reasoning.

sections.title: Suffering, gratuitous evil, and divine love
sections.rationale: The compatibility of apparently purposeless suffering with unlimited power and love is a motion-level dispute and the principal potential defeater confronting rational theism.

sections.title: Objective morality and its grounding
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether moral judgments arise adequately from natural processes or require God, and whether grounding goodness in divine nature avoids arbitrariness.

sections.title: Design, evolution, and human purpose
sections.rationale: Fine-tuning, biological complexity, evolutionary selection, and intentional human existence form a shared dispute over whether observed order and life support divine design.

sections.title: Revelation, miracles, and salvation confusion
sections.rationale: Disagreement about miracle claims, culturally inherited belief, biblical authority, and salvation requirements bears on what revelation an all-loving God should provide and whether religious assent is rational.

routes.description: Establish Christian belief as an intellectually defensible interpretation of shared evidence and as a morally constructive framework whose governing norms, explanatory resources, and characteristic effects cannot be reduced to pathological or extremist uses.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if religious interpretation remains epistemically permissible alongside science, offers a defensible basis for meaning and morality, and supplies internal norms and practices that distinguish constructive Christianity from coercive misuse.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defensibility of religious interpretation and the constructive operation of Christian moral norms to the motion's combined intellectual and moral standard.

centralBridges.description: Show that science does not exhaust questions of existence, meaning, and value, leaving Christian belief available as a contestable interpretation of public evidence.
Explain why transcendent grounding can support moral obligation and why secular alternatives face their own justificatory burdens.
Distinguish Christianity's governing norms from extremist capture and demonstrate how those norms can criticize violence, restrain dehumanization, and motivate forgiveness.
Provide principled interpretations of sacrifice and difficult scripture that preserve restoration and moral transformation without making coercion or violence normative.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Situate historical harms alongside evidence of well-being, generosity, and constructive conduct without treating beneficial effects as proof of theological truth.
Show that psychological desire neither establishes nor refutes belief and may shape religious and atheistic commitments alike.

routes.description: Establish that religious belief exceeds the available evidence and that claims of divine authority introduce coercive doctrines, permissions, and incentives that are unnecessary for morality and capable of worsening human harm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts better fit the public evidence, secular human capacities adequately ground moral life, and authoritative religious doctrines add distinctive mechanisms of coercion or harm without indispensable moral benefits.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential insufficiency and the harmful consequences of asserted divine authority to the motion's indictment of religion as unsupported and coercive.

centralBridges.description: Use cosmology, evolution, natural history, and explanatory parsimony to challenge anthropocentric design, intervention, revelation, and confident knowledge of divine commands.
Ground moral obligation in solidarity, reciprocity, and evolved social capacities while denying that religion supplies an indispensable or uniquely moral act.
Show how canonical texts, doctrines, and claimed divine commands can authorize conduct ordinarily judged cruel, coercive, or lethal.
Explain how surveillance, compulsory obedience, threatened punishment, salvation conditions, and eschatological authority make religious commitment coercive rather than freely optional.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate religious welfare or consolation effects from the truth of theological claims and from conclusions about religion's general moral character.
Answer secular atrocity comparisons by examining religious alliances and the transfer of faith, messianism, and unquestioned obedience into political movements.

sections.title: Public Evidence, Science, and Religious Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the intellectual half of the motion by comparing naturalistic accounts of cosmology and human history with the claim that science leaves legitimate room for transcendent meaning and Christian interpretation.

sections.title: Divine and Secular Grounds of Moral Obligation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether transcendent foundations are needed to justify moral judgments or whether solidarity, reciprocity, and evolved social capacities can sustain obligation without divine authority.

sections.title: Religious Harm, Extremism, and Constructive Effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether violence and social harm are characteristic consequences of religion or products of broader human and ideological extremism, while also testing the relevance and limits of claimed constructive effects.

sections.title: Scripture, Salvation, Sacrifice, and Coercive Authority
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether foundational texts and doctrines normalize sacrifice, punishment, and compelled obedience or admit principled interpretations centered on voluntary restoration and nonviolent moral correction.

sections.title: Consolation, Human Dignity, and Worldview Motivation
sections.rationale: This issue tests psychological explanations of belief and unbelief, including whether religion rests on consoling desire, degrades or elevates human dignity, or offers meaning without converting desire into evidence.

routes.description: Establish that natural science is a powerful but domain-limited mode of inquiry and that rational explanation also includes agency, purpose, normativity, historical inference, and an account of why an intelligible universe is accessible to rational minds.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one significant question worth explaining cannot be resolved by scientific mechanism alone and a distinct form of explanation is shown to be rationally applicable rather than merely filling a temporary empirical gap.

motionBridge.description: Show that explanations worth having are not exhausted by publicly testable natural mechanisms and that at least one additional explanatory category is rationally required.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish scientific descriptions of natural processes from explanations involving agency, purpose, meaning, or obligation.
Account for the rational intelligibility of nature and the reliability of minds that investigate it without presupposing that scientific method explains its own foundations.
Establish that claims about divine action, cosmic origin, or historically alleged miracles can be assessed through rational and evidential inquiry rather than excluded by definition.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how affirming natural regularities and scientific progress remains compatible with deeper purposive or agent-based explanation.
Connect the proposed wider explanatory framework to moral responsibility, human significance, and personal meaning.

routes.description: Establish science as the uniquely reliable route to reality, argue that its progressive natural explanations face no demonstrated terminal boundary, and show that purported alternatives either lack public evidence or project human concerns beyond what reality warrants.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if scientific inquiry can in principle cover every genuine evidential question while purpose, supernatural agency, objective normativity, and related alleged exceptions are either naturally explainable or not warranted as features requiring explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that every genuine question about reality is in principle answerable through evidence-governed scientific inquiry, with no established need for another explanatory kind.

centralBridges.description: Defend public evidence, testability, and mutually supporting natural explanations as the criteria for legitimate claims about reality.
Provide or motivate impersonal natural accounts of cosmic order, origins, cognition, life, and moral behavior without invoking divine agency.
Show that supernatural and purposive proposals do not add warranted explanatory content beyond natural inquiry.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use the continuing reach and precision of scientific progress to support confidence in eventual explanatory completeness.
Distinguish evidential questions about reality from projected human desires for cosmic purpose or permanent significance.

sections.title: The Scope and Standards of Rational Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue sets the motion-level framework by testing whether scientific evidence and mechanism exhaust legitimate explanation or coexist with irreducible explanations involving agents, purposes, and other rational categories.

sections.title: Scientific Progress, Intelligibility, and Rational Minds
sections.rationale: The competing accounts must explain both science's expanding success and the preconditions that make an orderly world knowable by evolved human cognition, including whether those preconditions support naturalism or a deeper source.

sections.title: Origins of Natural Law, the Universe, and Life
sections.rationale: Cosmic lawfulness, the emergence of a universe, and the boundary between prebiotic origins and biological evolution provide direct tests of whether natural explanation is sufficient in principle or leaves a foundational remainder.

sections.title: Miracles, Historical Evidence, and Revisability
sections.rationale: The resurrection dispute concentrates the clash over natural regularity, historical testimony, exceptional agency, and what observations could rationally revise either supernatural belief or disbelief.

sections.title: Morality, Purpose, and Human Meaning
sections.rationale: Moral obligation, shared values, cosmic purpose, and human significance test whether scientific and evolutionary accounts explain all relevant phenomena or only describe facts and behavior without grounding normativity or meaning.

routes.description: Establish that historically meaningful witness traces survived in the Gospel and resurrection traditions despite ordinary discrepancies, transmission, and theological interpretation, and that the total attestation warrants confidence beyond a purely visionary or literary origin.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source proximity and retained local knowledge support substantial continuity, that discrepancies and unusual narrative features are compatible with sincere witness-derived transmission, and that the resurrection evidence resists the proposed ordinary causal alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The combined documentary and resurrection evidence must justify substantial historical confidence in witness-derived traditions without requiring complete inerrancy.

centralBridges.description: Establish sufficient chronological, geographical, and cultural continuity between the narrated events and the surviving accounts.
Explain why contradictions and variations can arise within broadly truthful, independently transmitted testimony.
Show that the resurrection traditions’ content and effects are inadequately explained by ordinary visions or later apologetic construction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify how the quantity and independence of early attestation should affect confidence in extraordinary claims.
Account for doubt, misrecognition, physicality, and other resistant details as potential traces of unusual experiences.

routes.description: Establish that ordinary historical analysis supports only a limited reconstruction of Jesus and the rise of resurrection belief because the Gospels are late, dependent, anonymous, internally divergent, and shaped by oral transmission and theological controversy.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source relationships and contradictions limit independence and straightforward reliability, that historical method cannot privilege unprecedented supernatural explanations over familiar alternatives, and that visions plus theological reinterpretation explain resurrection belief and its narrative development.

motionBridge.description: The surviving evidence must support only bounded historical claims while leaving bodily resurrection historically unestablished.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate how dependence, authorship, dating, transmission, and contradiction constrain the Gospels’ evidentiary independence and accuracy.
Apply comparative historical probability to miracle reports without assuming either their impossibility or their occurrence.
Provide an ordinary causal account connecting post-crucifixion experiences, messianic reinterpretation, and emerging resurrection belief.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate well-supported baseline claims such as Jesus’s existence from less secure claims about particular deeds and sayings.
Explain difficult resurrection details through the narratives’ literary, theological, and polemical functions.

sections.title: Documentary Base, Dating, and Historical Proximity
sections.rationale: The identity, relationships, dating, and local knowledge of the surviving sources determine how closely their traditions can be connected to eyewitnesses and the events they narrate.

sections.title: Transmission, Variation, and Gospel Contradictions
sections.rationale: The debate must determine whether differences among the accounts are compatible with broadly truthful transmission or instead demonstrate alteration that materially limits historical confidence.

sections.title: Historical Method and Extraordinary Claims
sections.rationale: The standard used to compare miracle reports with ordinary alternative explanations governs whether strong attestation could ever support a resurrection or other unprecedented event.

sections.title: Experiences and the Origins of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of visions, messianic reinterpretation, missionary action, and the emergence of Christian belief bear directly on whether a bodily resurrection is required by the evidence.

sections.title: Resurrection Narratives: Witness Traces or Apologetic Development
sections.rationale: Doubt, misrecognition, empty-tomb material, physical demonstrations, and supernatural features must be assessed as either resistant experiential traces or products of later literary and theological debate.

routes.description: Establish at least one first cause by excluding causal loops and infinite regress, apply the causal principle to make that cause beginningless and initially changeless, distinguish it from material reality, and infer personal agency from its capacity to originate the universe without prior determination.
routes.successCriteria: The pro burden is satisfied if the defended causal structure and causal principle require at least one beginningless, transcendent first cause, and if originating a first change from an initially changeless condition warrants attributing libertarian agency and personhood to that creator.

motionBridge.description: Connect a beginningless and initially changeless first cause to a personal creator capable of freely originating the universe.

routes.description: Deny that the reformulated Kalam uniquely establishes its conclusion by challenging the exclusions and property inferences required for the creator route, presenting a necessary initial natural state as a rival foundation, and comparing the complete theories for consistency, explanatory coverage, and economy.

centralBridges.description: Show that the causal premises do not conclusively exclude regress or loops and at most yield one or more uncaused causes without the further creator properties.

sections.title: First Causes, Infinite Regress, and Causal Loops
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the causal series must terminate in at least one first cause and therefore supplies the indispensable starting point for either a creator inference or a universe-internal initial-cause account.

sections.title: The Causal Principle and a Necessary Initial Natural State
sections.rationale: The central clash is whether every beginning requires a cause or whether a metaphysically necessary initial natural state may begin causelessly while grounding the causal explanation of all later reality.

sections.title: Necessity, Possibility, and Ultimate Explanation
sections.rationale: The rival accounts depend on whether necessity can explain an initial state, whether beginninglessness supports necessity, and whether logically consistent alternatives count as metaphysically possible alternatives requiring selection.

sections.title: Beginninglessness, Timelessness, Events, and Change
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether the proposed first cause can coherently be timeless, beginningless, and initially changeless, and whether an initial event or state escapes or falls under the relevant causal principle.

sections.title: Personal Agency and Comparative Explanatory Burden
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately requires a bridge from a first cause to a personal creator, while the competing route asks whether libertarian agency adds explanatory value beyond a simpler universe-internal natural foundation.

routes.description: Establish reflective Christianity as credible through a cumulative case from philosophical reasoning, scriptural and experiential considerations, and resurrection evidence, while limiting skeptical inferences from evil, disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive considerations provide reasonable warrant for Christianity and the negative considerations neither render its core claims unlikely nor defeat the cumulative case when assessed together.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative positive case and the answers to skeptical objections to the conclusion that reflective Christianity remains credible.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments can provide discriminating support for theism despite uncertainty about premises, divine motivations, and evidential partitioning.
Show that revelation, religious experience, and resurrection considerations supply warrant for distinctively Christian claims rather than generic theism alone.
Show that evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and moral failure do not outweigh or defeat the positive cumulative case.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify when cognitive limits and consequential complexity legitimately restrict skeptical likelihood judgments without indiscriminately defeating positive arguments.
Distinguish reasonable Christian credibility from certainty and explain why acknowledged disagreement need not require an atheistic conclusion.

routes.description: Establish skeptical atheism by challenging the predictive and explanatory force of the positive Christian considerations and presenting evil, religious disagreement, expert dissent, and Christian moral failure as cumulative evidence against Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the positive arguments fail to make Christianity sufficiently probable and the negative considerations are better expected without the Christian account of God, revelation, resurrection, and transformation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the failure of the positive case and the cumulative skeptical evidence to the conclusion that Christianity is unlikely.

centralBridges.description: Show that philosophical arguments, biblical beauty, religious experience, and resurrection evidence lack the claimed discriminatory or explanatory force.
Show that apparently preventable suffering and persistent religious confusion are less expected under the proposed Christian God than under naturalism.
Show that informed dissent and the observed moral record materially reduce confidence in Christianity's truth and transformative claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply naturalistic explanations for fine-tuning and resurrection data that avoid disputed assumptions about divine psychology or miraculous intervention.
Require consistent treatment of uncertainty, cognitive limitation, comparative expertise, and likelihood reasoning across positive and negative arguments.

sections.title: Philosophical Arguments, Fine-Tuning, and Divine Psychology
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether philosophical and fine-tuning arguments predict a life-permitting universe under theism or instead depend on uncertain premises, contested value theories, and arbitrary evidential partitions.

sections.title: Scripture, Religious Experience, and Reflective Warrant
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether biblical qualities and religious experience distinguish Christian revelation and justify reflective belief despite rival experiences, counterarguments, and disagreement.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Naturalistic Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether physical resurrection best explains the burial, appearances, and resulting bodily-resurrection belief or whether a naturalistic sequence explains the same evidence.

sections.title: Evil, Religious Disagreement, and Epistemic Limitation
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether suffering and failed or uneven revelation are improbable under Christianity, and whether appeals to consequential complexity or cognitive limits answer those inferences consistently.

sections.title: Expert Dissent, Rational Confidence, and Christian Moral Fruit
sections.rationale: This issue examines how interdisciplinary and specialist disagreement should constrain confidence and whether Christianity's claimed moral transformation generates unmet observable expectations relevant to credibility.

routes.description: Establish that the universe began to exist, defend a causal principle whose metaphysical scope includes that beginning, and show that the resulting explanation can be a transcendent personal efficient cause without preexisting material conditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the universe's beginning falls under a defensible metaphysical causal principle, objections based on ordinary material and temporal causation do not establish an exemption, and conceptual analysis supports a transcendent personal cause.

motionBridge.description: Connect the universe's causally explained beginning to a cause beyond spacetime and material reality, with grounds for treating that cause as personal.

centralBridges.description: Establish that being cannot begin from nonbeing and that this principle is not restricted to processes occurring within spacetime.
Establish that the universe can genuinely begin even though no earlier temporal interval exists.
Establish the coherence and explanatory adequacy of efficient causation without a preexisting material cause.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require a relevant basis for exempting the universe from a principle applied to other things that begin.
Explain why allowing an uncaused universe would not license arbitrary substances to begin uncaused.

routes.description: Show that ordinary causal evidence supports principles governing physical processes within spacetime but does not warrant extending efficient causation to the beginning of spacetime and matter or inferring a transcendent personal creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the pro side does not justify metaphysical scope beyond observed causal conditions, narrower principles account for ordinary regularity, and the universe's temporal boundary does not independently require transcendent causation.

motionBridge.description: Show that causal regularities within the universe do not supply a warranted bridge to a transcendent cause of the universe.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the evidential basis for causation is bound to spacetime, material conditions, and interaction within physical reality.
Show that induction supporting efficient causes also supports material accompaniment, creating a parity problem for creation without matter.
Distinguish existence at every temporal point from an object appearing after an earlier interval in which it did not exist.
Provide restricted causal principles that preserve ordinary regularity without extending causation to the universe as a whole.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require an account of how causation remains intelligible when no preexisting thing is affected.
Show that a principled exceptional class need not entail arbitrary uncaused objects or unrelated spontaneous events.

sections.title: Physical or Metaphysical Scope of the Causal Principle
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether experience of causation within the universe can justify applying a causal premise to the origin of spacetime and material reality themselves.

sections.title: Material Accompaniment and Immaterial Agent Causation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether material involvement is essential to intelligible efficient causation and whether personal agency supplies a coherent model of causation without prior matter.

sections.title: Temporal Beginning and the Universe's Boundary
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether existence at every temporal point nevertheless constitutes coming into being and whether ordinary appearance-from-nothing intuitions transfer to the universe.

sections.title: Restricted Causal Principles and Ordinary Regularity
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether narrower causal rules can explain why ordinary objects do not begin uncaused while withholding commitment to an unrestricted metaphysical principle.

sections.title: Selective Uncaused Existence and the Arbitrary-Objects Challenge
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether allowing an uncaused universe makes arbitrary uncaused substances inexplicable, and whether exceptions for particular classes can answer that challenge.

routes.description: Establish that emergent spacetime, the character and apparent irreducibility of consciousness, and the need for an ultimate foundation jointly favor a fundamental conscious source over naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these features are warranted, their unification under fundamental consciousness offers sufficient explanatory scope and parsimony, and defeasible metaphysical inference can identify that conscious foundation as God despite underdetermination objections.

motionBridge.description: Show that the total evidence makes a fundamental conscious source identified as God more reasonable than the available naturalistic accounts.

centralBridges.description: Connect emergent spacetime and informational structure to features for which a mind-first ontology supplies a unified explanation.
Establish that subjective consciousness is not adequately reduced to or produced by matter and therefore points toward fundamental mentality.
Explain why the necessary or regress-ending foundation should be conscious and why that foundation may properly be identified as God.
Defend comparative metaphysical inference as legitimate without requiring certainty, while applying parsimony only among explanatorily sufficient accounts.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why consensus and methodological naturalism do not by themselves exclude minority interpretations or mind-first explanations.
Account for brain-consciousness correlations without treating correlation alone as proof that neural activity produces subjective experience.

routes.description: Establish that the cited scientific, phenomenological, and cosmological considerations do not discriminate theism from naturalistic pantheism or other provisional natural accounts, while divine attributes add unsupported commitments.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the pro evidence remains equally compatible with non-theistic alternatives, ordinary inquiry cannot justify the required unrestricted divine properties, and naturalistic accounts retain adequate comparative simplicity and explanatory possibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available evidence does not make theism more reasonable when non-theistic alternatives accommodate it without the same divine commitments.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate that evidence shared by theism and non-theistic alternatives cannot, without an additional discriminator, support theism specifically.
Distinguish fallible empirical justification from warrant for absolute metaphysical properties and require support for the latter.
Provide a comparative basis for expecting undiscovered natural explanations of spacetime and consciousness rather than positing fundamental cosmic mentality.
Require that added personal, moral, and maximal properties earn explanatory necessity rather than functioning as unrestricted auxiliary assumptions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend methodological naturalism as provisional and revisable inquiry rather than a commitment that supernatural reality is impossible.
Test the divine conclusion against natural ultimate-origin alternatives and against implications associated with perfect power and goodness.

sections.title: Emergent Spacetime, Quantum Information, and Cosmic Mind
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the debate's principal scientific considerations positively indicate mentality at reality's foundation or remain compatible with nonconscious emergence and established physical inquiry.

sections.title: Consciousness, Reduction, and Idealist Ontology
sections.rationale: The status of subjective experience is a central bridge from observations about minds to idealism, while the competing burden is to explain why unresolved consciousness does not warrant a new fundamental ontology.

sections.title: Abduction, Knowledge Limits, and Metaphysical Inference
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether limited and fallible evidence can support comparative conclusions about an ultimate conscious foundation and its properties without demanding certainty or exceeding human justification.

sections.title: Underdetermination, Explanatory Scope, and Parsimony
sections.rationale: The motion turns on whether theism explains the shared evidence better than pantheism and other alternatives, requiring comparison of discriminating power, explanatory adequacy, and the cost of added attributes.

sections.title: Necessary Foundations, Cosmic Origins, and Divine Identification
sections.rationale: This issue addresses what terminates explanatory regress, whether broader natural cosmologies can fill that role, and what further reasoning is required to identify a foundational cause as a conscious God.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative route from libertarian agency and a caused temporal universe to a divine agent, then use historical resurrection claims to identify that agent with the Christian God while addressing hiddenness and revelation objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its generic theistic arguments warrant a personal divine cause, the resurrection inference supplies a specifically Christian identification, and the principal skeptical challenges do not defeat the cumulative evidential connection.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative philosophical and historical case to the existence of the specifically Christian God rather than merely an unspecified cause or deity.

centralBridges.description: Show that libertarian agency is real, required for rational and moral responsibility, and better explained by theism than by naturalistic determinism.
Show that the universe began to exist and that its cause is a timeless, immaterial, powerful agent rather than an unspecified impersonal condition.
Show that the relevant historical claims are adequately grounded and that divine resurrection explains them better than the principal naturalistic alternatives.
Explain why the available evidence and mode of divine disclosure are compatible with a Christian God seeking freely formed trust.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend philosophical and historical inference as legitimate methods for realities and past events not directly measurable by scientific instruments.
Preserve the supporting credibility of transmitted Christian sources and reported miracles against claims of pervasive corruption or evidential disappearance.

routes.description: Withhold belief in the Christian God by testing each component of the cumulative case for reliable support, Christian specificity, and explanatory discrimination, while treating hiddenness and inconsistent revelation as contrary evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if libertarian agency, the divine Kalam extension, and resurrection remain insufficiently established or non-unique, and if the expected clarity and consistency of Christian revelation are absent under reliable evidential standards.

motionBridge.description: Show that the offered arguments do not warrant belief in the specifically Christian God and that skepticism need not establish universal divine nonexistence.

centralBridges.description: Challenge both the evidence for libertarian freedom and its compatibility with an omniscient creator who knowingly selects a complete world history.
Separate the claim that the universe has a cause from unsupported conclusions that the cause is an agent, a God, or the Christian God.
Require historical and supernatural claims to rest on confirmable evidence and methods capable of distinguishing resurrection or divinity from natural, technological, or deceptive alternatives.
Show that sincere nonbelief, unclear disclosure, competing revelations, and textual uncertainty conflict with expectations generated by the proposed Christian God.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground rational skepticism in provisional confidence and claim-sensitive evidence without requiring absolute certainty or asserting the disputed proposition is false.
Test whether faith, philosophical inference, historical comparison, and miracle reports reliably discriminate true Christian claims from incompatible alternatives.

sections.title: Libertarian Freedom, Rational Agency, and Divine Foreknowledge
sections.rationale: This issue tests a foundational argument for God from experienced freedom, moral responsibility, and rational deliberation, together with the objection that libertarian choice is unverified or incompatible with divine creation and foreknowledge.

sections.title: Kalam and the Identity of the Universe's Cause
sections.rationale: This issue covers both the inference that the universe requires a cause and the further bridge from a temporal beginning to a timeless personal agent, including whether those added attributes uniquely support theism.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Christian Identification
sections.rationale: The resurrection is the principal bridge from generic theistic considerations to the specifically Christian God, making the status of the historical premises, alternative explanations, and antecedent miracle plausibility central to the motion.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness, Revelation, and Textual Reliability
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether sincere nonbelief, religious disagreement, ambiguous disclosure, and manuscript uncertainty count against the expected conduct of the Christian God or remain compatible with freely chosen trust and preserved revelation.

sections.title: Evidential Standards, Falsifiability, and Explanatory Discrimination
sections.rationale: This cross-cutting issue determines which philosophical, historical, empirical, and testimonial methods can warrant extraordinary conclusions and whether observed anomalies can discriminate divine action from unknown or deceptive alternatives.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The libertarian freedom people experience is better explained by God because a natural universe operating solely through physical cause and effect would be deterministic.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly introduces Hunter, and the uninterrupted first-person opening statement presents his announced affirmative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move initiates the affirmative agency route and therefore has no earlier opposing move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly advances a central route but compresses its naturalism-to-determinism bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but “natural system,” determinism, and the scope of physical causation are not sufficiently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling God the best explanation and appealing to what everyone knows substantially exceeds the supplied experiential and conceptual support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says a natural universe would be a system of cause and effect, that God could grant libertarian freedom, and that people know they could do otherwise.

moves.speaker: Braxton Hunter
moves.proposition: The disciples' reported experiences and willingness to die for their proclamation are better explained by God raising Jesus than by deliberate fabrication or disputed visionary-error accounts.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the announced historical bridge to Christian identification and has no prior opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly advances the motion-level identification route, though historical warrants remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The best-explanation claim is clear, but the evidential scope and comparison class of natural alternatives remain underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical best-explanation conclusion exceeds the displayed support for the reports, martyrdom premise, and rival exclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes willingness to die, disputes the antecedent dismissal of miracles through recalibrated plausibility, and concludes that God raising Jesus is the best explanation.

routes.description: Establish that compassion and other humane goods arise independently of religion, then show that religious doctrine, dogma, revelation, or institutional authority appropriates those goods while adding morally harmful conditions or obstructing reform.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to whether religion adds avoidable doctrinal harm to human goods that exist without it.

centralBridges.description: Establish that compassion, community, equality, and reforming concern can arise outside or prior to Christian doctrine.
Show that authoritative teachings or revelations introduce or entrench serious harms alongside claimed religious benefits.
Explain humane religious reform as movement away from specific harmful rules toward broader human compassion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test claims of Christian humanitarian causation against prolonged conduct under Christian institutional power.
Use concrete cases such as slavery, subordination, and conquest to test proposed religious moral foundations.

routes.description: Distinguish corrupt religion from Christianity's governing sacred ideals, locate domination in a general human condition, and show how Christian anthropology and devotion supplied foundations and institutions for universal compassion, equality, and reform.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian doctrines provide a coherent basis and historically consequential mechanism for humane ideals that cannot be reduced to unaided tribal concern, while apparent religious harms can be distinguished from or corrected by those doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to Christianity's capacity to originate, ground, and extend the humane ideals used to judge religious corruption.

centralBridges.description: Locate pride, violence, and domination in humanity generally rather than treating religion as their distinctive cause.
Ground equal human worth and moral obligation in divine love, the image of God, and the incarnation.
Trace sacred ideals into practices and institutions extending protection and compassion beyond kin, status, or tribe.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how Christianity contains standards for condemning corrupt religious power and interpreting difficult inherited practices.
Explain why moral condemnation requires a foundation stronger than present agreement or culturally contingent preference.

sections.title: The Governing Test: Prior Human Goods or Distinctive Religious Contribution
sections.rationale: This issue defines what the motion requires by testing whether acknowledged religious goods are uniquely generated by religion or are independently human goods burdened by harmful additions.

sections.title: Slavery, Abolition, and the Pace of Christian Reform
sections.rationale: Slavery supplies the debate's principal doctrinal and historical test of whether Christianity entrenched domination or furnished the anthropology and reforming trajectory that overcame it.

sections.title: Women, Family, and Christian Social Institutions
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of scripture, monogamy, and institutional change test whether Christian teaching constrained exploitation or imposed harmful subordination on women.

sections.title: Moral Grounding, Divine Love, and Equal Human Worth
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether humane judgments can stand on shared human concern alone or require the Christian account of divine goodness, love, and persons bearing sacred worth.

sections.title: Conquest Narratives, Revelation, and Religious Violence
sections.rationale: The Canaan narratives provide a concentrated test of whether revelation authorizes grave moral harm or can be interpreted within a framework that ultimately prohibits religious violence.

sections.title: Universal Compassion and Its Historical Sources
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether concern for outsiders, enemies, and the weak is an ordinary cross-cultural human capacity or a distinctively Christian ideal made socially expansive through doctrine and institutions.
